column2: Cardiogenic shock from critical AS: balloon aortic valvuloplasty temporarily relieves obstruction as a bridge to AVR/TAVI (restenosis within months).
Low-flow low-gradient AS with poor EF: dobutamine stress echo separates true severe AS (gradient rises, area stays ≤ 1 cm²) from pseudo-severe and shows contractile reserve.
In chronic severe AR diastolic pressure falls and pulse pressure widens; LV end-diastolic volume, stroke volume and afterload all increase.
Acute severe AR: nitroprusside (± dobutamine) increases forward flow as a bridge to surgery. IABP is contraindicated; beta-blockers lengthen diastole.
Rheumatic heart disease is by far the commonest cause of mitral stenosis/LV inflow obstruction worldwide; annular calcification in the elderly.
In MS left atrial pressure rises to drive flow across the valve; LV end-diastolic pressure is normal or low and output falls.
Anything raising heart rate or output raises LA pressure in MS. Beta-blockers (metoprolol) lengthen diastole and lower LA pressure.
In MS, LA pressure falls with diuretics, valvotomy, cardioversion or rate control. Pacing at 90/min shortens diastole and raises it.
MVA 1.7 cm² is moderate MS; asymptomatic with exercise PASP < 60 mmHg, so review and serial echo every 1–2 years.
In secondary (functional) MR surgery does not improve survival, but transcatheter edge-to-edge repair reduced mortality in selected patients (COAPT).
Diastolic gradients RA > RVEDP and wedge > LVEDP mean tricuspid and mitral stenosis; no systolic gradients exclude pulmonary and aortic stenosis.
Functional TR from pulmonary hypertension is treated by diuretics, salt restriction and pulmonary vasodilator therapy; valve surgery is high-risk.
Doming pulmonary valve with peak gradient > ~64 mmHg is congenital pulmonary stenosis: percutaneous balloon valvotomy.
New severe MR gives the LV a low-pressure outlet, so EF rises while forward flow and the aortic gradient fall.
AF with moderate–severe rheumatic MS needs warfarin (INR 2–3) regardless of CHA2DS2-VASc; rivaroxaban was inferior (INVICTUS).
Peripartum cardiomyopathy risk factors: older age, multiparity, twins, pre-eclampsia/hypertension, African ancestry. Primiparity is not one.
A wheelchair-bound young man with scoliosis and DCM has Duchenne muscular dystrophy (X-linked dystrophin); tall R in V1–V2 is typical.
Most familial cardiomyopathies are autosomal dominant missense mutations (MYH7, MYBPC3, TTN, LMNA); offer cascade screening.
TSH is part of routine tests in new heart failure, as hypo- and hyperthyroidism are reversible causes.
Fulminant lymphocytic myocarditis has a good outcome if supported (inotropes, ECMO/VAD); LV function often recovers fully.
Giant cell myocarditis (with autoimmune disease) progresses rapidly with heart block and VT; immunosuppression helps but many need urgent transplant.
Anthracycline cardiotoxicity rises with cumulative dose (> 400–450 mg/m²), chest radiotherapy, heart disease, age extremes and trastuzumab.
Viral pericarditis (rub, diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, normal troponin): high-dose aspirin or NSAID with PPI plus colchicine.
In tamponade inspiration increases RV filling (tricuspid inflow) while LV filling and SBP fall (pulsus paradoxus).
Pericarditis: diffuse concave ST elevation, PR depression, no reciprocal change or Q waves. ST elevation in V2 occurs in both, so it does not help.
Post-radiotherapy constriction (knock, dip-and-plateau) is treated definitively by pericardiectomy; diuretics give only temporary relief.
A pedunculated LA mass at the fossa ovalis with fever, arthralgia and TIA is myxoma: surgical excision without delay.
Melanoma has the highest propensity for cardiac metastasis; lung and breast cancer are commonest by number.
Commotio cordis: a precordial blow on the T-wave upslope triggers VF in a normal heart; immediate CPR and defibrillation save life.
Coronary artery disease is the leading cause of death in type 2 diabetes (2–4× risk, often silent ischaemia).
High-output heart failure in a heavy drinker that responds rapidly is wet beriberi from thiamine deficiency; give thiamine before glucose.
Hypothyroidism lowers heart rate, stroke volume and output, raises SVR and prolongs (not shortens) the QT.
Atherogenesis begins with LDL retention in the intima; oxidation, endothelial activation, monocyte recruitment and foam cells follow.
Arteries remodel outward, so a plaque does not narrow the lumen until it exceeds ~40% of the area within the internal elastic lamina (Glagov).
Statin benefit groups: clinical ASCVD, LDL ≥ 4.9 mmol/L, diabetes aged 40–75, 10-year risk ≥ 7.5%. Raised hs-CRP alone is not one.
HDL-raising drugs (CETP inhibitors, niacin, fibrates) did not cut events; weight loss and exercise improve HDL and overall risk.
Myocardial oxygen demand depends on heart rate, contractility and wall stress (preload and afterload); rhythm itself is not a primary determinant.
The heart already extracts ~70–75% of oxygen at rest, so extra demand is met by arteriolar dilatation and increased coronary flow.
Ischaemia shifts to anaerobic glycolysis: lactate and H⁺ accumulate (pH falls), ATP depletes, calcium rises and potassium leaks out.
Angina radiates to arms, neck, jaw, epigastrium and back; radiation to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericarditis.
Peaked T waves with flat P waves are hyperkalaemia: give IV calcium gluconate first, then insulin–glucose and salbutamol.
Long QT from ST-segment lengthening the day after thyroidectomy suggests hypocalcaemia (parathyroid injury): measure ionised calcium.
S4 is atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle, so it falls just after the P wave; S1 coincides with QRS. No S4 in AF.
Cardiogenic shock after MI: urgent PCI, with noradrenaline as first-line vasopressor (SOAP II), ± dobutamine. Routine IABP is not recommended.
Morphine is not recommended in acute heart failure, especially in shock (hypotension, respiratory depression, worse outcomes).
